# AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware Alignment Technique for Large Language Models

Sayantan Adak    Pratyush Chatterjee    Somnath Banerjee    Rima Hazra
   Somak Aditya    Animesh Mukherjee

###### Abstract

Present day LLMs face the challenge of managing affordance-based safety
risks—situations where outputs inadvertently facilitate harmful actions
due to overlooked logical implications. Traditional safety solutions,
such as scalar outcome-based reward models, parameter tuning, or
heuristic decoding strategies, lack the granularity and proactive nature
needed to reliably detect and intervene during subtle yet crucial
reasoning steps. Addressing this fundamental gap, we introduce AURA, an
innovative, multi-layered framework centered around Process Reward
Models (PRMs), providing comprehensive, step level evaluations across
logical coherence and safety-awareness. Our framework seamlessly
combines introspective self-critique, fine-grained PRM assessments, and
adaptive safety-aware decoding to dynamically and proactively guide
models toward safer reasoning trajectories. Empirical evidence clearly
demonstrates that this approach significantly surpasses existing
methods, significantly improving the logical integrity and
affordance-sensitive safety of model outputs. This research represents a
pivotal step toward safer, more responsible, and contextually aware AI,
setting a new benchmark for alignment-sensitive applications ¹¹ 1 Code
and Dataset: https://github.com/sayantan11995/AURA.

¹Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur, India

² Eindhoven University of Technology, Netherlands

³ Cisco Systems

## Introduction

In the physical world, certain situations may arise where performing
certain actions (or affordances) may incidentally cause physical or
materialistic harm to humans (or materials) involved in the situation.
Imagine a situation where John is driving a car, steering along a busy
road while simultaneously checking his phone to reply to a friend’s
text. In this scenario (illustrated in
Figure [1](#Sx1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Introduction ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")),
while John, the actor, may physically afford to drive and type
simultaneously; the action of typing (or messaging) may compromise his
safety (or that of other passengers) by drawing his concentration away
from the critical action (or affordance) of driving a car. Such
hypothetical risks may arise even while John’s action is being
influenced by the suggestions of an LLM-based personal assistant. For
example, if the LLM guiding John’s AI assistant fails to recognize the
implicit risk associated with responding immediately, suggesting John
reply right away, it inadvertently facilitates a hazardous situation. We
define this as an affordance-based safety risk, i.e., situations in
which model outputs implicitly encourage harmful actions due to
overlooked contextual possibilities and their logical
consequences ([Birr et al. 2024](#bib.bib5)).

![Refer to caption](2508.06124v1/affordance_front_new.png)

Figure 1: Risk-aware affordance in a real-world driving scenario;
conflicting affordances lead to a safety-critical decision point.

While LLMs continue to be very effective across a range of tasks, they
increasingly expose critical vulnerabilities, particularly in their
inability to adequately recognize and proactively address
affordance-based safety risks alongside maintaining logical
coherence ([Son et al. 2025](#bib.bib24); [Zhou et al.
2025](#bib.bib44)). The intersection of coherence and
affordance-sensitive safety becomes particularly crucial in nuanced,
real-world contexts, where discerning potential harm demands meticulous,
stepwise understanding of implicit logical implications²² 2
https://openai.com/index/chain-of-thought-monitoring/. Affordances
represent potential actions implicitly available in a given context, and
affordance-based safety pertains to an LLM’s capability to anticipate
and manage scenarios where its outputs may inadvertently enable harm.
Closely intertwined with coherence, the principle of maintaining logical
consistency throughout the reasoning steps, ensuring each inference
logically proceeds from the preceding one ([Wang et al.
2025b](#bib.bib30)) (see
Figure [1](#Sx1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Introduction ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")
showing the interplay of coherence and safety). In high-stakes
applications, such as healthcare, finance, automated decision-making,
and social interactions ([Zhai et al. 2025](#bib.bib36)), overlooking
affordance-based risks or failing to maintain coherence could propagate
misinformation, confusion, or tangible harm ([Son et al.
2025](#bib.bib24)). Consequently, developing robust mechanisms to
identify and mitigate these risks is not merely beneficial but
essential ([Zhang et al. 2025a](#bib.bib37)).  
Current approaches to managing these risks primarily involve
retrospective corrections like flagging problematic outputs after their
generation or scalar optimization strategies like Outcome-based Reward
Models (ORMs) ([Lyu et al. 2025](#bib.bib18)).ORMs fall short in
intricate logical reasoning tasks, where overlooking critical
intermediate steps limits proactive intervention. Similarly, parameter
tuning ([Hazra et al. 2024](#bib.bib10); [Banerjee et al.
2025a](#bib.bib2)) and decoding heuristics ([Banerjee et al.
2025c](#bib.bib4)) face substantial limitations due to their rigidity
and context insensitivity. To address these fundamental shortcomings, we
advocate a paradigm shift toward detailed, stepwise logical reasoning
assessment. Process Reward Models (PRMs) ([Zhang et al.
2025b](#bib.bib39)) have emerged as promising tools capable of
delivering granular, multi-dimensional evaluations, covering logical
coherence, affordance-sensitive safety awareness, and proactive
intervention opportunities. Our proposed system explicitly leverages
PRMs through introspective chain-of-thought (CoT) refinement, granular
intermediate reasoning assessments, and dynamic safety-aware decoding.
These components collectively steer the model away from potentially
hazardous or incoherent reasoning paths, embedding coherence and safety
deeply into the model’s reasoning processes.

Our main contributions include the following. • To the best of our
knowledge, we are the first to introduce AURA, a unique affordance-aware
PRM based alignment specifically tailored for fine-grained, step level
evaluation of coherence and safety within complex, context-rich logical
reasoning scenarios. Unlike prior PRM approaches, which predominantly
target structured, mathematically-defined reasoning domains ([Zhang
et al. 2025b](#bib.bib39); [Pala et al. 2025](#bib.bib20)), AURA
uniquely addresses nuanced affordance-sensitive risks in ambiguous,
real-world complex situations, enabling proactive intervention in unsafe
or incoherent reasoning trajectories. • We curate a robust
step-annotated dataset SituationAfford, comprising over $`2,550`$ unique
situations, $`7,506`$ harm-intent queries, and $`15,011`$ annotated
reasoning steps, constructed from realistic affordance contexts. •
First, through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that AURA achieves
state-of-the-art performance in step level safety and coherence
classification. Second, the safety rate for our PRM-guided response
generation is notably better compared to the base model generation
across multiple models. Finally, AURA generalizes effectively to
downstream generation tasks, reducing the relative Attack Success Rate
(ASR) by up to 50% on two different multi-turn jailbreak
benchmarks—validated via both automatic and human evaluation.

## Related work

Safety-sensitive reasoning and coherence in LLMs: Recent work
underscores the importance of coherent multi-step reasoning and safety
in high-stakes LLM deployments. The chain-of-thought monitorability
framework reveals CoT trace exposure as both essential and fragile for
identifying unsafe reasoning ([Korbak and Balesni 2025](#bib.bib12);
[Banerjee et al. 2025b](#bib.bib3)), while also highlighting trade-offs
between failure detectability and language drift. [Jiang et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib11) quantify safety risks in extended reasoning (e.g.,
math/code) and show that post-hoc classifiers often miss
context-sensitive affordance violations. Broader safety reviews echo
persistent vulnerabilities like prompt injection, misuse, and latent
reasoning errors³³ 3 https://encr.pw/TuCBv. In planning, affordances,
implicit action possibilities are often overlooked, leading to unsafe
outputs when models lack affordance-awareness ([Zhang et al.
2025b](#bib.bib39); [Choudhury 2025](#bib.bib7)). Together, these
insights advocate for real-time, inference-level safety interventions
over reactive output filtering.  
Reward modeling for process-aware reasoning: Alignment efforts have
shifted from scalar Outcome Reward Models (ORMs) to Process Reward
Models (PRMs) that assess reasoning steps for correctness, coherence,
and safety ([Zhang et al. 2025b](#bib.bib39)). PRMs expose step level
failures and outperform best-of-N baselines ([Zhao et al.
2025](#bib.bib40)). GenPRM enhances CoT with symbolic verification,
surpassing GPT-4 on math tasks ([Zhao et al. 2025](#bib.bib40));
Athena-PRM extends PRMs to multimodal reasoning ([Wang et al.
2025a](#bib.bib29)), while R-PRM achieves parity with large models using
only 15% of training data ([She et al. 2025](#bib.bib23)). DG-PRM
applies Pareto-dominant reward trees for improved generalization ([Yin
et al. 2025](#bib.bib34)), RetrievalPRM mitigates distribution shifts
via trace similarity ([Zhu et al. 2025](#bib.bib45)), and SP-PRM
combines process and outcome signals for 3.6–10.3% human-eval gains over
ORM-only methods ([Xie et al. 2025](#bib.bib33)).

![Refer to caption](2508.06124v1/affordance_main.png)

Figure 2: Schematic diagram of our method AURA.

## The overall architecture of AURA

We introduce AURA, a structured framework for affordance-based,
risk-aware alignment in LLMs. AURA mitigates unsafe completions by
intervening during the reasoning process itself, targeting stepwise
errors arising from misaligned affordances or incoherent logic. Instead
of relying on post-hoc filtering, AURA takes a two-staged approach: (i)
a self-critique-guided reasoning loop that revises candidate responses
based on safety-oriented feedback, and (ii) a reward-based trajectory
selection mechanism that ranks reasoning paths using a specialised
process reward model – AffordRanker. This integrated approach enables
the model to generate trajectories that are both contextually coherent
and aligned with situational affordances. We describe the overall
methodology, the construction of the SituationAfford dataset, and the
training process in the following sections.

### Preliminaries

We conceptualize the reasoning process in AURA as a structured
decision-making task, where the language model operates as a policy over
an abstract environment defined by natural language contexts. Formally,
we define the state space $`\mathcal{S}`$ such that each state
$`s\in\mathcal{S}`$ is a tuple $`(S,Q,\mathcal{H})`$, comprising a
textual situation $`S`$, a query $`Q`$, and a reasoning history
$`\mathcal{H}=\{r_{1},\ldots,r_{j-1}\}`$ of prior steps. The action
space $`\mathcal{A}`$ consists of atomic reasoning steps $`r_{j}`$,
where each step represents a single proposition that advances the
reasoning toward answering the query. The reward space is captured by a
structured function $`\mathcal{R}_{p}(s,a_{j})=(E_{pc},E_{av})`$, where
$`E_{pc}`$ denotes the procedural coherence score—reflecting logical
consistency with earlier steps—and $`E_{av}`$ denotes the affordance
validation score—indicating whether the step respects contextual safety
constraints. The policy model $`\mathcal{M}_{p}`$, instantiated as an
instruction-tuned LLM, takes a state $`s`$ and stochastically generates
the next action $`a_{j}\in\mathcal{A}`$, corresponding to a reasoning
step $`r_{j}`$, conditioned on the current situation, query, and step
history. A complete reasoning trajectory $`R=\{r_{1},\ldots,r_{t}\}`$ is
thus a sequence of such actions, which we evaluate using a Process
Reward Model (PRM)—referred to as AffordRanker. This model computes
per-step error vectors ($`\mathbf{ev}_{j}`$) and aggregates them to
produce a cumulative score
$`\mathcal{RW}(R)=\frac{1}{t}\sum_{j=1}^{t}(E_{\text{pc}}^{(j)}+E_{\text{av}}^{(j)})`$,
which is used to rank and select the most coherent and safe trajectory.

### Overall framework

AURA follows a two-stage alignment framework that guides generation
through critique and structured reward. First, it produces
self-critique-conditioned reasoning trajectories via $`\mathcal{M}_{p}`$
that reflect safety feedback from itself (self-critique). Then, it ranks
and selects the most reliable response using a reward model trained to
capture stepwise affordance coherence. We describe each stage in detail
below. A schematic for the overall setup is shown in
Figure [2](#Sx2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Related work ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models").  
Self-critique-conditioned reasoning: We construct self-critique ([Wen
et al. 2025](#bib.bib31); [Valmeekam, Marquez, and Kambhampati
2023](#bib.bib28); [Gou et al. 2024](#bib.bib9)) conditioned reasoning
trajectories by prompting the policy model $`\mathcal{M}_{p}`$, which we
define as the language model responsible for generating stepwise
reasoning given a situation and a query, with its own safety feedback.
Instead of applying iterative corrections, we embed the critique as a
conditioning signal within the input prompt. Given a situation $`S`$ and
a query $`Q`$, the policy model $`M_{p}`$ generates two initial
reasoning trajectories $`R_{1}^{0}`$ and $`R_{2}^{0}`$, each comprising
a stepwise explanation and a final answer. These responses serve as
first-pass attempts, which the model then critiques to identify
potential flaws in reasoning and affordance violations. It produces a
critique rationale $`\mathcal{RS}`$ and a refined answer $`A`$, which we
append to the original inputs to form an augmented prompt
$`\mathcal{P}_{aug}`$. This prompt encodes safety-aware preferences and
guides the generation of improved candidate responses in the subsequent
reward-based selection phase. This phase is shown in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Overall framework ‣ The overall architecture of AURA ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")
(see Step 1).  
Reward-based trajectory selection: Once we have the augmented prompt
$`\mathcal{P}_{aug}`$ through self-critique, we sample a set of $`N`$
candidate reasoning trajectories
$`{R_{1}^{1},R_{2}^{1},\dots,R_{N}^{1}}`$ from the policy model
$`\mathcal{M}_{p}`$. Each trajectory $`R_{i}^{1}`$ consists of a
sequence of $`t`$ reasoning steps that attempt to answer the given query
based on the provided situation. To evaluate and select the most
reliable trajectory, we use AffordRanker, which performs step level
reward assessment focused on reasoning quality and affordance alignment.
AffordRanker takes each reasoning step $`r_{j}`$ from a trajectory
$`R_{i}^{1}`$ and produces two scalar values: a procedural coherence
score $`E_{pc}`$ that measures the logical consistency of $`r_{j}`$ with
respect to the prior reasoning steps, and an affordance validation score
$`E_{av}`$ that quantifies how well $`r_{j}`$ aligns with the contextual
constraints and affordances present in the situation. We provide
detailed definitions and modeling of procedural coherence score and
affordance validation score in the next subsection. For each trajectory,
we compute the cumulative reward $`\mathcal{RW}(R_{i}^{1})`$ as the
average of the total stepwise scores (see line number 17-21 in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Overall framework ‣ The overall architecture of AURA ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")).

Input: Situation $`S`$, Query $`Q`$, policy model $`\mathcal{M}_{p}`$  
Output: $`\boldsymbol{R}_{\boldsymbol{\text{best}}}`$

1: Step 1: Self-critique-conditioned reasoning.

2: // Generate initial independent responses

3: $`R_{1}^{0},R_{2}^{0}\leftarrow\mathcal{M}_{p}(S,Q)`$

4: // Obtain critique rationale $`\mathcal{RS}`$ and answer

5: $`\mathcal{RS},A\leftarrow\mathcal{M}_{p}(S,Q,R_{1}^{0},R_{2}^{0})`$

6: // Augment base prompt with self critique

7:
$`\mathcal{P}_{aug}\leftarrow\text{concat}(S,Q,R_{1}^{0},R_{2}^{0},\mathcal{RS},A)`$

8: Train AffordRanker

9: $`\mathcal{M}_{aff}\leftarrow train\_PRM\_model();`$
$`\triangleright`$ Base: Qwen-2.5-7B

10: Step 2: Reward based trajectory selection

11: // Generate $`N`$ number of independent responses from
$`\mathcal{M}_{p}`$

12:
$`\{R_{1}^{1},R_{2}^{1},\cdots R_{N}^{1}\}\leftarrow\mathcal{M}_{p}(\mathcal{P}_{aug})`$

13: // Obtain the rewards for the responses

14: for $`i=1`$ to $`N`$ do

15:   $`E_{PC}=0`$, $`E_{AV}=0`$

16:   for $`j=1`$ to $`t`$ do

17:    // Rewards for each step $`r_{j}`$ of response $`R_{i}^{1}`$

18:    $`E_{pc}`$, $`E_{av}\leftarrow\mathcal{M}_{aff}(r_{j})`$

19:    $`E_{PC}`$ += $`E_{pc}`$, $`E_{AV}`$ += $`E_{av}`$

20:   end for

21:   $`\mathcal{RW}(R_{i}^{1})=\frac{1}{t}(E_{PC}+E_{AV})`$

22: end for

23: // Rank the responses $`\{R_{1}^{1},R_{2}^{1},\ldots,R_{N}^{1}\}`$
by descending final reward score $`\mathcal{RW}(R_{i}^{1})`$

24: $`R_{\text{best}}\leftarrow\arg\max_{i}\mathcal{RW}(R_{i}^{1})`$

25: return $`\boldsymbol{R}_{\boldsymbol{\text{best}}}`$

### The design of the AffordRanker

A Process Reward Model (PRM) evaluates multi-step reasoning chain of a
response by assigning rewards at the level of individual reasoning steps
(see Step 2 of
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Overall framework ‣ The overall architecture of AURA ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")).
Unlike conventional reward models that assess the final output in
isolation, a PRM operates over the full trajectory, scoring each
intermediate step based on its contribution to coherent, goal-directed
reasoning. Given a query $`Q`$ and a sequence of reasoning steps
$`{r_{1},r_{2},\ldots,r_{t}}`$ of a response $`R`$ generated by a policy
model, the PRM computes a reward for step $`r_{j}`$ as

|     |                                                          |     |     |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle R_{j}=\text{PRM}(Q,r_{1},\ldots,r_{t})`$ |     | (1) |

Here, PRM denotes the process reward model, and $`R_{j}`$ reflects how
well the $`j`$-th step maintains logical consistency with previous steps
and supports progress toward answering the query. By providing step
level supervision, PRMs enable fine-grained control over the reasoning
process and facilitate more robust alignment than output-only evaluation
schemes.

While traditional PRMs combine multiple reasoning signals into a single
scalar, we explicitly disentangle reward types to capture distinct
dimensions of reasoning quality. This separation allows us to diagnose
both the nature of coherence errors and their implications for safety.
Specifically, we define two primary error categories, each associated
with a corresponding reward component: – (a) procedural coherence errors
($`E_{pc}`$): This error reflects a breakdown in the progression of
reasoning steps. It arises when a step deviates from the expected
inferential path—by skipping intermediate steps, introducing unsupported
conclusions, or failing to preserve continuity with prior context (see
Figure [1](#Sx1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Introduction ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")
for an example); (b) affordance violation errors ($`E_{av}`$): A
reasoning step that introduces or relies on an affordance likely to
result in unsafe or harmful outcomes. This includes assumptions about
actions or entities that, while possible, violate implicit safety
constraints of the environment or task.

By assigning rewards along these two axes, our model provides a
structured and interpretable evaluation of each reasoning step.
Figure [1](#Sx1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Introduction ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")
illustrates examples of both error types. We train the AffordRanker
using a carefully curated dataset SituationAfford, which we describe
next.

### The SituationAfford dataset

We construct the SituationAfford dataset with fine-grained, step level
annotations to train AffordRanker (denoted by $`\mathcal{M}_{aff}`$)
used in Step 2 of our framework. Each reasoning step $`r_{j}`$ in a
trajectory is annotated with a binary error vector
$`\mathbf{ev}_{j}=(E_{pc},E_{av})`$, where $`E_{pc},E_{av}\in\{0,1\}`$
indicate whether the step violates procedural coherence ($`E_{pc}=1`$)
or safety affordance ($`E_{av}=1`$), respectively. The overall dataset
creation process involves: (i) textual situation generation, (ii) query
generation and categorisation, (iii) step level SituationAfford dataset
annotation, and targeted data augmentation. These annotated trajectories
enable $`\mathcal{M}_{aff}`$ to learn step level reward signals that are
later aggregated into the final trajectory score
$`\mathcal{RW}(R_{i}^{1})`$, used for ranking in the inference stage.

|                 |                  |                  |                  |
| --------------- | ---------------- | ---------------- | ---------------- |
| Category        | Valid trajectory | $`E_{pc}=1`$ (%) | $`E_{av}=1`$ (%) |
| goal-based      | 5,100            | 10,644 (29.9%)   | 11,136 (31.2%)   |
| property damage | 4,964            | 10,506 (30.4%)   | 17,382 (50.2%)   |
| physical harm   | 4,947            | 10,480 (30.7%)   | 18,742 (54.8%)   |
| Total           | 15,011           | 31,630 (30.3%)   | 47,260 (45.0%)   |

Table 1: Projected step level coherence and safety label distribution
per reasoning category, assuming each category spans 5100 samples
(situation + query + reasoning steps). Some samples got discarded by
GPT-4o. Percentages are relative to the total steps for that category.

|                                                                |         |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| \#Trajectories in the training set                             | 12,009  |
| \#Trajectories in the val/test set                             | 1,501   |
| \#Step level annotated instances in training data              | 131,391 |
| \#Step level annotated instances in val/test data (balanced)   | 16,422  |
| \#Step level annotated instances in val/test data (imbalanced) | 20,848  |

Table 2: Summary of dataset composition in training, validation and test
splits across whole trajectories and at step level. Note that, in the
balanced setting we undersampled the prominent label.

(a) Situation generation: To construct the SituationAfford dataset, we
leverage two existing resources: (a) MSSBench ([Zhou et al.
2024](#bib.bib43)) and (b) Text2Afford ([Adak et al. 2024](#bib.bib1)).
From MSSBench, we extract 186 unique unsafe contexts originally designed
for multimodal safety evaluations. Complementarily, we incorporate 2,369
natural language descriptions from Text2Afford, each encoding an
object-centric affordance context suitable for generating diverse
situational prompts. To enrich these contexts with realistic dynamics,
we design a generation prompt that expands each input into a 250-word
scene narrative⁴⁴ 4 We use  250-word situations to provide sufficient
context for multi-step safety reasoning and prevent refusal from LLM
having two human activities. This setup encourages affordance conflict
situations where the action of one agent implicitly limits or
contradicts the other’s. Such interactions naturally surface violations
of implicit safety norms and expose weaknesses in step-wise reasoning.
These generated narratives, combined with curated unsafe contexts, form
the basis of the procedural and affordance-related errors $`E_{pc}`$ and
$`E_{av}`$ at the step level, as noted in the previous section.  
(b) Query generation and categorization: For each generated situation
$`S`$, we construct prompts to elicit sensitive queries spanning three
harm intent categories, adapted from MSSBench ([Zhou et al.
2024](#bib.bib43)): (i) goal-based, (ii) property damage, and (iii)
physical harm. We define an affordance violation as any case where the
model implicitly assumes that an unsafe or infeasible action is valid
within the given physical or situational context. The intent categories
can be briefly described as follows –goal-based queries are generic and
task-oriented without explicit harmful intent, property damage queries
imply intentions to harm objects or surroundings, while physical harm
queries encourage actions that could endanger individuals, even if the
risk is only implicit. This structured categorization supports targeted
evaluation of affordance failures across varying levels of risk.
Examples can be found in
Section [A](#A1 "Appendix A Data example ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")
in the supplementary material. For each situation, we generate three
queries per harm category using a prompt⁵⁵ 5 The detailed prompts for
each of the stages are illustrated in
Section [E](#A5 "Appendix E Prompts ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")
in the supplementary material. that includes a single in-context example
from the corresponding MSSBench category. We iteratively refine these
prompts through controlled manual tuning to ensure semantic coherence
and category alignment, consistent with standard few-shot prompting
practices ([Le Scao and Rush 2021](#bib.bib14); [Liu et al.
2021](#bib.bib16); [Zhao et al. 2021](#bib.bib41)). To ensure quality,
we apply automated filtering using GPT-4o ([OpenAI and Team
2024](#bib.bib19)) to remove non-harmful or trivial outputs, followed by
manual verification to validate their alignment with the intended harm
categories.  
(c) Reasoning trajectory generation: Given a situation-query
($`S`$-$`Q`$) pair, we construct prompts to elicit two alternate
reasoning trajectories from the policy model $`\mathcal{M}_{p}`$. Each
trajectory consists of up to seven steps⁶⁶ 6 Each trajectory contains
seven reasoning steps to ensure consistent supervision and capture
evolving safety dynamics without excessive annotation overhead (see
Section [B](#A2 "Appendix B Data construction details ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")
in the supplementary material for details)., where each step expresses a
single, concise fact or action that is logically consistent with prior
steps and advances the response toward answering the query. Steps must
incorporate both explicit and implicit elements from the context, avoid
redundancy, and reflect a distinct human activity. We generate the
entire sequence in a single pass using a structured prompt, as shown in
Section [E](#A5 "Appendix E Prompts ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")
in the supplementary material.  
(d) Stepwise label annotation and data augmentation: For each generated
trajectory, we annotate every reasoning step with two binary labels:
$`E_{pc}`$ for procedural coherence errors and $`E_{av}`$ for affordance
violation errors. We use GPT-4o to generate these annotations
synthetically. To label a specific step $`r_{j}`$, we construct an input
prompt that includes the situation, the query, and all preceding steps
$`{r_{1},\ldots,r_{j-1}}`$. We iteratively refine the prompt design to
ensure that the annotations are both consistent and aligned with our
reward signal definitions. To further ensure label reliability, we apply
a secondary verification step using an LLM-as-a-judge framework, where
we discard the instances having at least two incorrect step level
judgements. The structured prompt for the LLM is provided in
Section [E](#A5 "Appendix E Prompts ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")
in the supplementary material. Samples with label vectors that conflict
with the judge model’s decision are discarded to maintain overall
dataset quality.

The final SituationAfford dataset comprises 2550 unique situations, 7506
harm-intent queries, and 15011 annotated reasoning trajectories,
resulting in a total of 208,862 step level annotations (see
Table [1](#Sx3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ The SituationAfford dataset ‣ The overall architecture of AURA ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")).
After the annotation was completed, we found an imbalance between
positive ($`E_{pc}=1`$/$`E_{av}=1`$) and negative
($`E_{pc}=0`$/$`E_{av}=0`$) instances across both error dimensions. To
mitigate this, we perform label balancing by downsampling
overrepresented positive samples and augmenting the underrepresented
negative class. For augmentation, we perturb selected valid reasoning
steps to introduce incoherence or affordance-inconsistent behavior,
preserving grammaticality while injecting subtle logical or contextual
flaws. This augmentation strategy improves the model’s ability to detect
nuanced failures in reasoning, especially within affordance-sensitive
scenarios. We partition the dataset in an 8:1:1 split for training,
validation, and test sets, respectively (see
Table [2](#Sx3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ The SituationAfford dataset ‣ The overall architecture of AURA ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")
for exact counts).  
Manual validation: To assess the reliability of our synthetic
annotations, we conduct a human validation study using the Prolific⁷⁷ 7
https://www.prolific.com/ platform. A total of 33 qualified annotators
participated in the process. We randomly sampled 50
situation-query-response instances from each category of queries from
our dataset, and got them independently annotated by three annotators.
Annotators had to first determine whether the query was harmful given
the situation, and then evaluate the response across four dimensions:
safe and helpful, unsafe but helpful, safe but not helpful, and unsafe
and not helpful⁸⁸ 8 Detailed instructions can be found in
Section [B](#A2 "Appendix B Data construction details ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")
in the supplementary material.. We observe high agreement on query
harmfulness (Fleiss’ $`\kappa=0.83`$) and moderately high agreement on
response evaluation (Fleiss’ $`\kappa=0.62`$), with the query identified
as harmful for 86% of the cases and the most frequent response label
being safe and helpful. We observe in 87% of cases the annotators marked
the response as helpful (safe + unsafe). These results validate the
integrity of our dataset and confirm that our affordance-sensitive
annotations reflect human-aligned safety and helpfulness judgments. Full
instruction to the annotators is provided in the
Section [B](#A2 "Appendix B Data construction details ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")
in the supplementary material.

### Training procedure

We implement our AffordRanker ($`\mathcal{M}_{aff}`$) using
Qwen-2.5-7B-instruct ([Qwen et al. 2025](#bib.bib22)) as the base model,
chosen for its strong performance on tasks involving multi-step,
safety-aware reasoning. Unlike prior approaches that replace the
language modeling head with a scalar regression head ([Zhang et al.
2025b](#bib.bib39); [Xia et al. 2025](#bib.bib32); [Tan et al.
2025](#bib.bib26)), we preserve the model’s original architecture to
maintain its generative flexibility. To support step level supervision,
we extend the tokenizer with two additional control tokens,
$`\langle+\rangle`$ and $`\langle-\rangle`$, used to mark positive and
negative labels for individual steps during training. To train
$`\mathcal{M}_{aff}`$, we convert each annotated reasoning trajectory
into a set of supervised instances. For a trajectory with $`t`$ steps,
we extract $`(t-1)`$ training instances by iterating over each step
$`r_{j}`$ for $`j=2`$ to $`t`$. Each instance includes the situation
$`S`$, the query $`Q`$, the sequence of prior steps
$`{r_{1},\ldots,r_{j-1}}`$, and the current step $`r_{j}`$. The model is
trained to generate a label vector $`(E_{pc},E_{av})`$ for $`r_{j}`$
based on this context. We apply this formulation consistently across all
harm categories (i.e., goal-based, property damage, and physical harm
scenarios). The full training prompt format is provided in the
supplementary material.

Table 3: Step level performance (F1 score) comparison of models under
balanced and imbalanced settings. Best results are highlighted. ^(∗)
indicates statistically significant improvement from the best baseline
using Mann-Whitney U test with $`p<0.05`$

We evaluate the effectiveness of AURA in guiding safer and more coherent
reasoning using both our curated dataset and external multi-turn safety
benchmarks. Our evaluation comprises three components: (i) step level
prediction accuracy of AffordRanker, (ii) quality of reward-guided safe
response generation, and (iii) the defense capability against multi-turn
jailbreak attacks.  
Evaluation of AffordRanker: We first assess the performance of
AffordRanker using the SituationAfford dataset. We construct two
evaluation setups as follows – balanced setting: This setup contains an
equal number of positive and negative test instances (16,422 annotated
steps) for each reasoning dimension (coherence and safety) matching the
class distribution used during training, and imbalanced setting: This
setup reflects real-world conditions without explicit balancing, where
naturally occurring class imbalance is preserved (20,848 annotated
steps). We use F1-score as the metric for each label category –
coherence and safety – under both balanced and imbalanced evaluation
settings.  
Reward-guided safe response generation: Given a situation and query, we
use AffordRanker to score multiple reasoning trajectories and select the
one with the highest cumulative reward (using the approach mentioned in
line 24 of the
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Overall framework ‣ The overall architecture of AURA ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")),
enabling search-based decoding aligned with coherence and safety. We
evaluate safety rate across varying depths (e.g., AURA@2, @4, @8), and
compare against baseline generation, and AURA without self-critique.
Safety rate is computed by comparing a model’s generated response
against the two annotated 7-step trajectories from SituationAfford. For
base generations, we directly compare to the ground truth; for
AffordRanker-guided search, we select the top-ranked response (as
described in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Overall framework ‣ The overall architecture of AURA ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")).
An LLM-as-judge (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B) is used to determine
whether the output is equally safe or safer than ground truth, defining
safety rate as

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\textit{safety rate}=\frac{\text{\#responses judged as safe or safer}}{\text{\#total number of instances}}
``` |  | (2) |



Defense capabilities: To assess the generalisation and real-world
robustness, we apply our reward-guided inference to two benchmarks
datasets – CoSafe ([Yu et al. 2024](#bib.bib35)) and STREAM ([Kuo et al.
2025](#bib.bib13)). CoSafe does not include step level annotations and
so we adapt it for our evaluation by treating each dialogue-query pair
as input and measure the ASR⁹⁹ 9 Safety rate is not applicable here due
to the absence of annotated $`\mathbf{ev}_{j}`$ vectors.. STREAM offers
more diverse and compositional attack types across varying dialogue
lengths. Here again, we evaluate ASR under different response generation
strategies.

For both these datasets, in order to measure ASR, we score each response
by GPT-4o on a scale from 1 (extremely unsafe) to 10 (completely safe).
We count an attack as successful if the score is below 5. Thus, we have

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{ASR}=\frac{\text{\# responses with score}<5}{\text{Total number of responses}}.
``` |  | (3) |

This metric allows us to quantify how often a model fails to resist
adversarial or harmful queries. The detailed evaluation prompts are
shown in the
Section [E](#A5 "Appendix E Prompts ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")
in the supplementary material.

## Experimental setup

We conduct extensive evaluations using a diverse set of baselines and
model configurations to benchmark the performance of AURA across both
step level safety classification and reward-guided safer response
generation tasks.

Baselines for step level evaluation: We compare AURA’s AffordRanker for
coherence and safety classification, against multiple strong
discriminative PRMs as follows – PathFinder-PRM-7B, ([Pala et al.
2025](#bib.bib20)), RLHFlow-Mistral-8B, RLHFlow-DeepSeek-8B¹⁰¹⁰ 10
https://github.com/RLHFlow/RLHF-Reward-Modeling, and ReasonEval-7B ([Xia
et al. 2025](#bib.bib32)). We follow a thresholding approach to convert
predicted reward scores into binary labels, consistent with prior work
such as ([Pala et al. 2025](#bib.bib20)). None of these models are
explicitly optimized for safety-sensitive affordance reasoning. To
compare against models tuned explicitly for safety, we consider
Beaver-7B-v1.0-cost and Beaver-7B-v3.0-cost ([Dai et al.
2024](#bib.bib8)), trained with human preference data emphasizing safe
response generation.
Policy models for reward-guided generation: We use five medium-sized
(7B–9B) instruction-tuned LLMs as base policy models for the
reward-guided safer response generation task – mistral(7b)-v0.3-inst,
gemma2(9b)-it, internlm3(8b)-inst, qwen2.5(7b)-inst, and
llama3.1(8b)-inst. We set the decoding parameters as follows:
temperature = 0.7, top-$`p`$ = 0.95, and maximum tokens = 512. For
self-critique generation, we reuse the policy model itself. For
PRM-guided decoding, we generate $`k\in\{2,4,8\}`$ response trajectories
and select the one with the highest average PRM score as the final
output.
Defense capability: For the ASR evaluation, we use the same five base
models and generation settings as above. For AffordRanker-guided
inference, we sample 8 response candidates per query and apply step
level reward scoring to rank and select the most coherent and safe
response.

Figure 3: Overall F1 score against the training data scales of different
baselines and AURA.

## Results

Step level evaluation:
Table [3](#Sx4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Evaluation ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")
presents a comparative analysis of various models on step level
coherence and safety classification under both imbalanced and balanced
settings. The proposed AURA model achieves the best overall performance,
substantially outperforming both discriminative baselines and
safety-aligned models, with F1 scores of 0.88 for coherence and 0.82 for
safety in the balanced setting. Crucially, AURA maintains consistently
high performance even in the imbalanced evaluation scenario—closely
mirroring real-world distributions—where it still achieves F1-scores of
0.83 (coherence) and 0.81 (safety) respectively. This highlights AURA’s
strong generalization ability and resilience to label skew, a key
requirement for deployment in safety-critical settings. Among
discriminative PRMs, models such as PathFinder-PRM-7B and
RLHFlow-DeepSeek-8B show moderate effectiveness, with overall F1-scores
below 0.70, indicating limited capacity to capture nuanced
affordance-sensitive violations. Safety-aligned models like
Beaver-7B-v3.0-cost perform reasonably well on safety detection (0.65),
but do not support coherence assessment, as they are not trained for
multi-step reasoning.
Figure [3](#Sx5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Experimental setup ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")
shows that AURA outperforms competing baselines in safety assessment,
even when those models are trained with 2–3$`\times`$ more data.
Reward-guided response generation:
Table [4](#Sx4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Evaluation ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")
reports the safety rate of model responses under different generation
strategies across five diverse policy models. We observe a consistent
and substantial improvement in safety when integrating both
self-critique and PRM-guided search over the base generation. The base
models, when used alone, yield relatively low safety rates (e.g., 0.11
for llama-3.1(8b)-inst and gemma-2(9b)-it), highlighting their
vulnerability to unsafe completions despite instruction tuning.
Incorporating self-critique offers modest gains across all models (e.g.,
+0.19 for qwen2.5(7b)-inst, +0.23 for internlm3(8b)-inst), but this
effect is significantly amplified when coupled with AffordRanker.
Specifically, using $`k=8`$ yields the highest safety rates across all
models, with internlm3(8b)-inst reaching 0.80 (+0.38) and
qwen2.5(7b)-inst reaching 0.71 (+0.43). These results confirm the
effectiveness of the AURA framework in navigating toward safer reasoning
trajectories through reward-guided decoding. Finally, the steady upward
trend from AURA@2 to AURA@8 further supports the hypothesis that deeper
sampling coupled with step level scoring leads to more reliable safety
alignment.
General defense capabilities:
Table [5](#Sx4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Evaluation ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")
reports the ASR across three benchmarks: CoSafe, STREAM, and our
proposed SituationAfford dataset. Across all models and datasets, we
observe a consistent reduction in ASR when incorporating our PRM, with
the full AURA pipeline achieving the lowest ASR in every setting.
Improvements are particularly pronounced on the SituationAfford
benchmark, where AURA reduces ASR by up to 50% relative to the base
model, underscoring its effectiveness in affordance-sensitive safety
scenarios. The performance gap between only PRM and AURA further
highlights the synergistic benefit of integrating reward-guided decoding
with self-critique.
Figure [4](#Sx5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Experimental setup ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")
shows the average category-wise ASR for all the categories for the
CoSafe dataset using: 1. Base model, 2. Only PRM, 3. AURA (ours),
highlighting the highest ASR in the Drug-Abuse category.
Manual evaluation: To complement the automated safety rate analysis, we
conduct a manual evaluation using a random sample of total 100 response
pairs across all policy models, comparing base generation and AURA@8
outputs. 5 human annotators with prior experience in LLM safety
assessment, recruited via Prolific, independently assess which response
in each pair is safer, based on the context and query. Aggregated
results show that responses guided by AffordRanker are judged safer in
81% of the comparisons, with substantial agreement among annotators
(Fleiss’ $`\kappa=0.72`$). This human preference further supports the
reliability of our reward-guided decoding strategy in producing safer,
more aligned completions.

Similarly, to validate the reliability of automated ASR scoring, for
each dataset, we randomly sample 50 instances—25 generated by the base
model and 25 by AURA—and present them in randomized, blinded pairs to 10
independent annotators. Annotators are asked to select the response that
appears safer in each pair. Aggregated results show that AURA-generated
responses are preferred in 82% of the comparisons, closely aligning with
the automated ASR trends.

## Discussion

### Stepwise performance

We perform a stepwise analysis of AffordRanker’s safety prediction
performance across the seven reasoning steps in each trajectory.
Interestingly, we observe a U-shaped performance trend (see
Figure [5](#Sx7.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Stepwise performance ‣ Discussion ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")),
with the highest F1-scores at the initial (Step 1: 0.94) and final steps
(Step 7: 0.93), and relatively lower performance in the middle steps
(Step 2–4: $`\sim`$0.73–0.76). This suggests that the model performs
well when initiating and concluding reasoning chains, likely due to
clearer contextual anchoring or summarization cues, whereas intermediate
steps pose greater challenges due to evolving context, causal
dependencies, and a higher likelihood of subtle transitions or
affordance shifts. The recovery in later steps may reflect the model’s
ability to re-align with safe reasoning as the trajectory stabilizes.

Figure 5: Stepwise analysis of AffordRanker’s safety prediction
performance across the seven reasoning steps.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Model Variant | Coherence (Imb.) | Safety (Imb.) | Coherence (Bal.) | Safety (Bal.) | Overall |
| AURA (Full) | 0.83 | 0.81 | 0.88 | 0.82 | 0.83 |
| AURA (Coherence only) | 0.82 | 0.73 | 0.87 | 0.74 | 0.79 |
| AURA (Safety only) | 0.81 | 0.80 | 0.85 | 0.81 | 0.82 |

Table 6: Ablation study showing the effect of using only coherence or
only safety reward for response selection. Combining both scores (top
row) leads to the best balance between coherence and safety.

### Error analysis

To better understand the limitations of our approach, we conduct both
quantitative and qualitative error analyses of AffordRanker’s step level
predictions.
Quantitative error analysis: We analyze false positive and false
negative rates across sampled examples from the query categories:
goal-based, property damage, and physical harm. We observe that the
lowest error rates occur in the goal-based category, where safety risks
are typically minimal or abstract. AffordRanker misclassifies fewer than
12% of cases, with a balanced precision-recall trade-off. In contrast,
the property damage category exhibits a significantly higher error
rate—false positives and false negatives together account for over 16%
of cases. This indicates difficulty in distinguishing between object
interactions that are contextually benign versus those that pose a risk
of damage, often due to subtle affordance shifts. The highest
misclassification rate is observed in the physical harm category, with
over 28% errors. This suggests challenges in detecting implicit or
multi-agent risk factors associated with physical injury, particularly
in dynamic or evolving situations.

Overall, these results suggest that AffordRanker is more reliable in
abstract or goal-directed settings, but still prone to safety
misjudgments in scenarios that require nuanced affordance interpretation
or implicit risk reasoning, albeit better than the state-of-the-art
methods available.
Qualitative error analysis: We conduct a qualitative inspection of
representative misclassifications to uncover recurring patterns in
AffordRanker’s failure modes for stepwise risk assessment. Most of the
errors arise from incorrect safety predictions, while coherence being
reliably detected. We categorize the observed safety-related errors as
follows.

- •
  Implicit risk: AffordRanker often fails to recognize danger when the
  risk is implied rather than explicit. For example, it misses the
  safety concern in the step “hiking on the exposed ridges during a
  thunderstorm,” despite the hazardous environmental cues.
- •
  Surface-level fluency: Steps that are well-written or instructional in
  tone are occasionally marked as safe, even when embedded in risky
  contexts. For instance, tactical football suggestions are rated as
  safe while players are exposed to lightning in an open field.
- •
  Multitasking and affordance conflict: The model struggles with
  scenarios involving dual affordance conflicts, such as discussing a
  movie while driving or glancing at a phone. These require reasoning
  about cognitive load and situational risk jointly.

These findings highlight AURA’s limitations in reasoning over latent
threats and multi-agent dynamics. Future enhancements could integrate
commonsense spatio-temporal modeling and explicit affordance graphs to
mitigate these issues.

### Ablation studies

#### Effect of individual reward dimension.

To understand the contribution of individual reward dimensions, we
perform ablations by using only coherence or only safety rewards during
inference for the step level evaluation conducted on the SituationAfford
dataset. As shown in
Table [6](#Sx7.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Stepwise performance ‣ Discussion ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models"),
using only the coherence reward yields comparable coherence performance
(within 0.01 of full model) but results in a noticeable drop in safety
F1-scores (up to 0.08 in the imbalanced setting), indicating that
coherence alone is insufficient to guide models toward safer reasoning.
Conversely, using only the safety reward retains strong safety alignment
and exhibits only a marginal decline (0.01–0.03) in coherence,
suggesting that safety guidance inherently captures some coherence
signals. These results confirm that combining both rewards provides a
synergistic benefit, achieving stronger and more balanced performance
across reasoning dimensions.

#### Effect of each component in reward-guided safer response generation

Table [7](#Sx7.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Effect of each component in reward-guided safer response generation ‣ Ablation studies ‣ Discussion ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models")
presents an ablation analysis on the impact of self-critique and
PRM-guided search in reward-guided response generation. Using only PRM
(without critique) improves safety marginally over base generation (0.26
vs. 0.22), while using only self-critique has a larger effect (0.38).
However, combining both components leads to substantial gains, achieving
0.65 safety rate at $`k=8`$, confirming that AffordRanker and critique
work synergistically to identify safer trajectories. The performance
consistently increases with search depth, suggesting deeper sampling
allows better exploitation of reward-guided diversity.

| $`{\color[rgb]{0.85,0,0}\textbf{A}}{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0}\textbf{U}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.4}\textbf{R}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0.8}\textbf{A}}{}_{\setminus\textsc{AffordRanker}}`$ | Self-critique only | 0.38 |

presents an ablation analysis comparing the impact of using only
self-critique, only PRM (k=8), and their combination in AURA on average
ASR. While both self-critique and PRM individually lower ASR compared to
the base generation, self-critique shows a stronger effect on the
SituationAfford dataset $`(0.42\rightarrow 0.28)`$, likely due to its
contextual nature. In contrast, PRM guidance proves more effective on
structured benchmarks like CoSafe and STREAM. The full AURA pipeline
consistently achieves the lowest ASR across all datasets, highlighting
the complementary strengths of self-reflection and step level reward
supervision in suppressing harmful generations.

| Setting | CoSafe ↓ | STREAM ↓ | SituationAfford ↓ |
| Base Generation | 0.17 | 0.18 | 0.42 |
| $`{\color[rgb]{0.85,0,0}\textbf{A}}{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0}\textbf{U}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.4}\textbf{R}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0.8}\textbf{A}}{}_{\setminus\textbf{Self-critique}}`$ | 0.13 | 0.14 | 0.35 |
| $`{\color[rgb]{0.85,0,0}\textbf{A}}{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0}\textbf{U}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.4}\textbf{R}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0.8}\textbf{A}}{}_{\setminus\textsc{AffordRanker}}`$ | 0.10 | 0.11 | 0.28 |
| AURA (Full) | 0.09 | 0.10 | 0.24 |

Table 8: Ablation on average ASR: Lower is better. Both self-critique
and PRM reduce attack success individually, while their combination in
AURA achieves the best defense across all benchmarks.

## Conclusion

We introduced AURA, an affordance-aware, risk-sensitive alignment
framework leveraging process-level supervision via Process Reward Models
(PRMs) for LLM reasoning. By integrating introspective self-critique,
fine-grained PRM assessments, and adaptive safety-aware decoding, AURA
dynamically steers reasoning toward safer trajectories, outperforming
traditional scalar outcome-based reward models and heuristic approaches.
We developed the SituationAfford dataset, comprising fine-grained step
annotations across diverse situational contexts, demonstrating
state-of-the-art performance in step-level safety and coherence. At
inference, our PRM-guided approach significantly improved safe response
rates and reduced attack success across multi-turn safety benchmarks.
Future directions include explicit modeling of latent and multi-agent
risks via affordance graphs, expanding multimodal integration to further
enhance reliability in safety-critical applications.

## Appendix B Data construction details

The instructions for the manual evaluation of the dataset are
represented in the
Figures [6](#A2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Why 7 reasoning steps? ‣ Appendix B Data construction details ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models"),
[7](#A2.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Why 7 reasoning steps? ‣ Appendix B Data construction details ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models"),
and
[8](#A2.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Why 7 reasoning steps? ‣ Appendix B Data construction details ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models").
We are providing the rationales for choosing the different backbones for
the construction of the SituationAfford below.

### Why MSSBench and Text2Afford datasets for situation construction?

MSSBench provides a curated set of real-world, multimodal situations
paired with queries designed to challenge language model safety
boundaries. While originally designed for multimodal input (text +
image), its chat subset includes text-only contexts with implicit safety
risks across domains like driving, household hazards, and social
behavior. We select this subset because:

- •
  It offers realistic and diverse unsafe scenarios, including complex
  agent-object interactions.
- •
  Its intent-driven queries are naturally aligned with our goal of
  reasoning over user queries that may be indirectly harmful or
  goal-oriented.
- •
  It provides a standard baseline in recent LLM safety evaluations,
  enabling comparative benchmarking.

Text2Afford is a structured dataset of natural language sentences
annotated with physical affordance categories (e.g., “cuttable,”
“drivable,” “graspable”) grounded in human-object interaction. We chose
this dataset because:

- •
  It provides affordance-centred contexts, ideal for generating
  situations where safety implications stem from physical object
  properties.
- •
  Its coverage of actionable verbs and object affordances enables
  simulation of realistic but subtle safety conflicts, e.g., texting
  while driving, placing flammable items near heat sources, etc.
- •
  It helps diversify the contextual space beyond overtly unsafe scenes,
  introducing affordance-sensitive queries that are otherwise
  underrepresented in conventional safety datasets.

Together, MSSBench and Text2Afford offer complementary benefits: the
former focuses on intent-level safety risks, while the latter anchors
scenarios in object-centric affordance reasoning. This combination
allows us to systematically explore safety reasoning across a wide range
of user intents, physical interactions, and environmental cues—making
SituationAfford a rich and generalizable benchmark for process-level
safety assessment.

### Why 250 words for situations?

We intentionally constrain each situation description to approximately
250 words to balance realism, contextual richness, and model
compatibility. In safety-critical domains, short or underspecified
contexts often fail to ground the harmful nature of a query, leading
models like GPT-4o to either decline response generation or produce
overly generic completions. Through iterative piloting, we found that
longer contextual descriptions improve the model’s capacity to reason
about situational dynamics, affordance conflicts, and subtle causal cues
over multiple steps. A 250-word narrative provides sufficient detail to
embed multiple human activities, environmental signals, and implicit
risks—without exceeding the processing limits of 7B–9B LLMs used in our
experiments. This length also aligns with realistic use cases such as
incident reports, situational assessments, or scenario planning ([Levy,
Jacoby, and Goldberg 2024](#bib.bib15); [Cheng et al. 2024](#bib.bib6);
[Lu et al. 2025](#bib.bib17)).

### Why 7 reasoning steps?

We adopt 7-step reasoning structure for several reasons:

- •
  Comparability and supervision granularity: Fixed-length step sequences
  enable consistent supervision, model alignment, and evaluation across
  all samples. This mirrors methodologies used in prior work, such as
  PRMBench ([Song et al. 2025](#bib.bib25)) and ProcessBench ([Zheng
  et al. 2025](#bib.bib42)), where uniform step windows enhance the
  robustness and reproducibility of PRM training.
- •
  Coverage of evolving safety dynamics: In safety-sensitive reasoning,
  risks typically emerge gradually—through accumulations of context,
  conflicting actions, or delayed consequences. Seven steps provide
  ample space for such dynamics to unfold, enabling coherent build-up,
  escalation, and intervention. In fact, our stepwise performance
  analysis
  (Section [Discussion](#Sx7 "Discussion ‣ AURA: Affordance-Understanding and Risk-aware AlignmentTechnique for Large Language Models"))
  reveals a U-shaped trend where intermediate steps (Steps 2–4) are more
  error-prone—indicating this middle window is where most safety
  reasoning complexity resides.
- •
  Practicality vs. annotation utility trade-off: Seven steps strike a
  balance between annotation effort and coverage of safety-relevant
  phenomena. Pilot studies indicated that most harmful reasoning arcs
  are adequately captured within 5–8 steps. Fixing to 7 allows for broad
  expressivity without overburdening human annotators or training
  pipelines.

While we adopt a fixed-length structure for experimental consistency,
our method is inherently agnostic to sequence length and can be extended
to variable-length reasoning in future work—potentially through adaptive
truncation or confidence-based step termination.

## Appendix C Extended evaluation setup

We carefully select model baselines and generation configurations to
ensure a comprehensive and fair evaluation of AURA across both safety
classification and reward-guided generation tasks. Below, we elaborate
on the rationale behind each choice.

### Discriminative PRM baselines

Our selection of PathFinder-PRM-7B, RLHFlow-Mistral-8B,
RLHFlow-DeepSeek-8B, and ReasonEval-7B represents a diverse spectrum of
state-of-the-art process reward models trained for multi-step reasoning
tasks. These models differ significantly in training regimes—ranging
from synthetic math-style reasoning to open-domain logical
validation—thereby offering valuable contrast points for evaluating
AffordRanker’s safety-specific reasoning capability. Importantly, none
of these baselines are explicitly optimized for affordance-sensitive
safety alignment, making them ideal comparators to quantify the gains
introduced by our affordance-aware approach.

To contrast with safety-aligned reward models, we include
Beaver-7B-v1.0-cost and Beaver-7B-v3.0-cost, which are trained on
extensive human preference data with an explicit focus on safe behavior.
These baselines help isolate the effect of reward models trained for
generic safety alignment versus those trained specifically on step-level
reasoning grounded in affordances.

### LLM-as-judge selection

For LLM-based evaluation of coherence and safety, we use
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B as the default judge model. This choice is
motivated by its superior cost-effectiveness, fast inference
capabilities, and reliable performance in prior safety alignment tasks
([Zhang et al.](#bib.bib38) ). We find that its decisions are
well-aligned with human annotator judgments, as confirmed in our manual
evaluations. While larger GPT-based judges may offer marginally higher
alignment in some domains, they pose practical limitations in scaling,
latency, and open deployment. Our selection therefore reflects a
pragmatic balance between judgment quality and reproducibility.

### Policy model diversity

We use a diverse pool of five open-source, instruction-tuned LLMs
spanning three model families (Qwen, Mistral, LLaMA, InternLM, and
Gemma) and parameter ranges (7B–9B). This design choice ensures that
AURA is evaluated in a model-agnostic fashion across architectures with
different inductive biases and decoding styles. These models also
represent state-of-the-art performance in lightweight
instruction-following and reasoning tasks ([Qi et al. 2024](#bib.bib21);
[Team 2024](#bib.bib27)) , making them strong base policies for
safety-sensitive generation.

### Reward-guided search depth ($`k`$)

We use $`k\in{2,4,8}`$ response samples in reward-guided search to
investigate the impact of search depth on safety alignment. This range
strikes a balance between computational cost and trajectory diversity,
allowing us to observe consistent improvements with deeper search (as
seen in Table 3 of the main text). Based on empirical trends and prior
work (e.g., R-PRM ([She et al. 2025](#bib.bib23)) , Pathfinder-PRM
([Pala et al. 2025](#bib.bib20)) ), we set $`k=8`$ as the default value
for AffordRanker-guided decoding in our final results, as it yields the
best trade-off between performance and sampling overhead.

## Appendix D Computing infrastructure

All experiments are conducted on an NVIDIA DGX Station A100 equipped
with $`4\times`$ NVIDIA A100-SXM4 GPUs (80GB each) and an AMD EPYC 7742
64-Core CPU. The system has 503 GB of system RAM and runs Ubuntu 20.04.6
LTS with Linux kernel version 5.4.0-212-generic, with models executed
using PyTorch 2.7.0 and the Hugging Face Transformers library version
4.53.1. Tokenization was handled via the tokenizers library (v0.15.0),
vLLM 0.9.2 and model inference was accelerated using DeepSpeed, while
GPT-4o, accessed through the OpenAI Python SDK (v1.3.8), served as data
synthesizer and ASR evaluation. All models, including Mistral-7B, and
LLaMA(3.1)-8B, were run in deterministic inference mode with fixed seeds
and a temperature of 0.0 to ensure reproducibility and consistency
across trials.

Training of AffordRanker is performed using a per-device batch size of 1
with gradient accumulation over 32 steps, effectively simulating a batch
size of 32. We use a learning rate of $`1\text{e}{-5}`$ with a cosine
scheduler and $`10\%`$ warmup ratio, training for 5 epochs. Model
checkpoints are saved every 1000 steps with only the latest model
retained. All experiments use a fixed random seed (42) for
reproducibility, mixed-precision training with bfloat16, and gradient
clipping set to a maximum norm of 1.0.
````
